title: Lab 3 – Addison & adrenal insufficiency
html:
Source: LP 3.pdf – 6 pages

Addison disease- causes #1

  •  Autoimmune adrenal insufficiency (AAI) - may be associated with other conditions in
  • Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndromes (Type 1- hypoparathyroidism, chronic
  • candidiasis, AAI; Type 2- AAI, autoimmune thyroid disease, T1DM)
  •  Infiltrations: amyloidosis, hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis
  •  Infections: Tuberculosis, fungal infections, CMV, HIV
  •  Adrenal hemorrhage/infarction: anticoagulant therapy, Waterhouse–Friderichsen
  • syndrome (meningococcal septicemia)
  •  Adrenoleukodystrophy- abnormal accumulation of very long chain fatty acids (VLCFAs)
  • in the brain, adrenal cortex, testes, and liver
  •  Iatrogenic: Bilateral adrenalectomy
  • Drugs: ketoconazole, abiraterone, etomidate and aminoglutethimide (inhibit
  • cortisol biosynthesis), mitotane (adrenolytic)
  • Addison disease- clinical picture
  •  Hyperpigmentation (skin+ mucous membranes)- absent in central adrenal insufficiency
  • - increased in sun-exposed areas and accentuated over pressure areas (knuckles, toes,
  • elbows, knees)
  •  General weakness and fatigue, malaise, weight loss (-> 15 kg), arthralgia, myalgia
  •  Gastrointestinal symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea/constipation, abdominal pain,
  • salt craving, anorexia
  •  Cardiovascular symptoms: Hypotension, orthostatic symptoms: dizziness, syncope.
  • !! Positive Schellong test (↓SBP of at least 20 mmHg or DBP of at least 10 mmHg within 3
  • min of standing).
  •  Hypoglycemia (→ sweats, tremor, headache)
  •  Irritability, emotional instability, depression
  •  Loss of axillary and pubic hair in men (↓ secretion of adrenal androgens).
  • Addison disease- diagnosis (2-step approach)
  • First step: assessing the adrenal cortex function -> paired cortisol and ACTH measurements
  • 1) Cortisol- Undetectable serum cortisol is diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency, primary
  • (PAI) or secondary (SAI), while a cortisol >20 μg/dL (550 nmol/l) precludes the diagnosis.
  • ! In equivocal cases (when uncertainty exists whether or not partial PAI is present) a rapid
  • ACTH stimulation test (Synacthen) may be necessary.
  • 2) ACTH- useful in differentiating pituitary causes (secondary forms) from adrenal causes of
  • adrenal insufficiency as follows:
  •  In primary adrenal insufficiency-> plasma ACTH levels are elevated.
  •  In pituitary ACTH deficiency (secondary hypoadrenalism), plasma ACTH levels are
  • inappropriately normal or less than 10 pg/mL (2.2 pmol/l).
  • Other tests: DHEA, DHEAS, androstenedione ↓; aldosterone ↓, plasma renin activity ↑;
  • serum electrolytes: ↓ Na, ↓ Cl, ↑ K

Second step: etiology #2

  •  Adrenal autoantibodies (e.g. antibodies to 21-hydroxylase)
  •  Imaging- Abdominal CT scan with contrast:
  • - Adrenal enlargement, with or without calcification- suggesting tuberculosis,
  • infiltration, or metastatic disease.
  • - Small and atrophic adrenals in chronic autoimmune adrenalitis.
  •  Percutaneous CT-guided adrenal biopsy → if metastatic lesions are suspected
  •  Specific tests- e.g. for TB (QuantiFERON, pulmonary X ray)
  • Other laboratory investigations: - Hypoglycemia
  • - Serum electrolytes: hyponatremia and hyperkalemia
  • - FBC: normocytic, normochromic anemia (altered androgen metabolism),
  • neutropenia, eosinophilia, and a relative lymphocytosis (lack of cortisol)
  • - High BUN and serum creatinine (volume depletion and dehydration).
  • Addison disease- PAI treatment
  • Patients with PAI require lifelong steroid replacement therapy (glucocorticoids and
  • mineralocorticoids) and often ↑ intake of NaCl to compensate for increased renal loss.
  • a) GC: Hydrocortisone (HC)- oral replacement in a dose of 15–25 mg/day: twice to thrice
  • daily, (e.g. 10 mg-5 mg-5 mg)
  •  Alternative: Prednisone 5–7.5 mg/day.
  • b) MC: Fludrocortisone (Astonin H) 0.1 mg/tb, 0.05–0.2 mg/day
  • c) DHEA replacement (25–50 mg/day) may improve mood, well-being, libido in women
  • Diet—↑ in proteins, vitamins, adequate dietary sodium intake
  • Patient education- how to increase GC dose in stressful situations:
  • • During period of minor stress → the daily dose of HC should be doubled (or 3×).
  • • During periods of major stress, such as a surgical procedure- the dose needs to be ↑
  • to as much as 200–400 mg HC/day
  • Adrenal crisis= EMERGENCY
  • Cause: Exposure of patients with Addison to stress (infections, trauma, surgery, dehydration)
  • Clinical picture: hypotension and shock, volume depletion, dehydration, hyperpyrexia,
  • weakness, apathy, depressed mentation, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, muscle
  • cramps, hypoglycemia. Shock and coma may rapidly lead to death in untreated patients.
  • Lab: ↓Na, ↑K, lymphocytosis, hypoglycemia, ↑ urea and creatinine ↑, metabolic acidosis +
  • ↓↓ CORTISOL. Do not wait for lab results if the clinical features are strongly suggestive!
  • Treatment: • IV 0.9% saline and 5% glucose are administered to correct volume depletion
  • • Hydrocortisone-> intravenously-100 mg followed by 50–75 mg every 6 h; when the patient is
  • stable, reduce the dosage to 50 mg every 6 h (MC= not necessary during the acute
  • replacement period); taper to maintenance therapy by day 4 or 5 and add mineralocorticoids.
  • • Identify and treat precipitating factor (e.g. infection).

Cushing syndrome- types and causes #3

  • The ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome- chronic ACTH hypersecretion->hyperplasia of the
  • adrenal zona fasciculata+ reticularis ->increased secretion of cortisol, androgens, DOC.
  •  ectopic ACTH/CRH syndrome (carcinoid tumors of lung, non-small cell and small cell
  • carcinoma of the lung, neuroendocrine tumors)
  •  Cushing disease (excessive pituitary ACTH secretion from a pituitary adenoma)
  • The ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
  •  primary adrenal neoplasm (adenoma or carcinoma), nodular adrenal hyperplasia
  •  iatrogenic (most commonly)- chronic GC therapy (orally, inhalator, topically).
  • Pseudo-Cushing- overactivation of the HPA axis, hypercortisolism is not autonomous
  •  psychiatric conditions (depression, anxiety, obsessive compulsive disorder), morbid
  • obesity, DM, alcoholism or eating disorders such as anorexia and bulimia nervosa
  • Cushing syndrome- clinical picture
  •  Central obesity: truncal+ buffalo hump, supraclavicular fat pads, moon face
  •  Skin changes: atrophy of the epidermis+ connective tissue, facial plethora, red-purple
  • striae (abdominal, breasts, hips), easily bruised following minimal trauma,
  • mucocutaneous fungal infections, acne, hirsutism.
  •  Cardiovascular effects: hypertension- DBP may be>100 mmHg, high risk of VTE
  •  Muscle weakness (proximal and especially in lower extremities), osteoporosis
  •  Reproductive dysfunction
  • F: menstrual irregularities, signs of virilization: hirsutism, alopecia, acne
  • M: ↓ libido, impotence ± some degree of gynecomastia; ↓body hair and soft testes
  •  CNS and psychological disturbances: emotional liability, anxiety, depression, poor
  • concentration, poor memory; euphoria, severe depression, psychosis with delusions or
  • hallucinations, paranoia, suicide.
  •  Metabolic: IGT/DM, hyperlipidemia, hypercalciuria (with kidney stones)
  • Cushing syndrome- diagnosis (2-step approach)
  • First step: Confirming the presence of Cushing syndrome
  • - Urinary free cortisol (UFC) (at least two measurements)
  • - Late-night salivary cortisol (two measurements); alternative: midnight serum cortisol
  • - 1-mg overnight DST (Bricaire test) = the best screening test
  • !! Two of these tests should be abnormal for Cushing syndrome confirmation.
  • !! Longer low-dose DST (Liddle 2x2) = the optimal test for those with psychiatric problems,
  • morbid obesity, alcoholism
  • Second step: Testing for the cause of Cushing syndrome
  • a) Plasma ACTH 8–9 a.m= to distinguish between ACTH-dependent/ independent forms
  • • ACTH ↓ (<10 pg/mL) ACTH-independent Cushing’s syndrome confirmed → the next step
  • = adrenal imaging studies (abdominal CT scan with contrast = first choice)
  • ⇒

• ACTH ↑ (frequently >52 pg/mL) or inappropriately normal ACTH secreting neoplasm-> #4

  • the next step= High-Dose DST (Liddle Test: 2 × 8) → for distinguishing pituitary causes from
  • ectopic ACTH production.
  • ⇒
  • Alternative: Overnight high-dose (8 mg) DST
  • b) Imaging
  •  Pituitary cause suspected: MRI of the pituitary gland with gadolinium enhancement
  •  Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor- imaging for localizing the tumor. Most of them are in the
  • thorax-> high-resolution chest CT is useful-> tumor not found-> CT of abdomen+ pelvis
  • Other Laboratory Findings
  •  ↓ TSH and thyroid hormones, gonadotrophins, gonadal steroids, GH (hypercortisolism
  • suppresses the thyroidal, gonadal, and GH axes)
  •  High normal Hb, Ht and red cell counts, ↓ lymphocytes and eosinophils
  •  Hyperglycemia, ↑ cholesterol and triglycerides, ↑Na, ↓ K
  • Cushing syndrome- treatment
  • Cushing’s Disease
  •  Transsphenoidal selective adenectomy= first choice!
  • Other options:
  •  Pituitary radiation therapy- control of cortisol levels may take months to years
  •  Medical treatment:
  • - Directed medical treatment (acts directly on corticotroph tumor cells to inhibit ACTH
  • production): Cabergoline (1–7 mg/week) and Pasireotide (0.6–0.9 mg subcutaneously
  • twice daily).
  • - Inhibitors of steroidogenesis: ketoconazole, levoketoconazole, metyrapone
  •  Bilateral adrenalectomy: in patients with very severe ACTH-dependent disease who
  • cannot be promptly controlled by surgery, radiotherapy or medical therapy
  • o life-long replacement treatment with GC and MC is needed thereafter
  • o risk of developing enlargement of the tumor and hyperpigmentation- Nelson’s
  • syndrome. Prophylactic radiotherapy ↓ the likelihood of this complication.
  • Adrenal Adenomas
  • - unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy; the outlook is excellent.
  • Adrenal Carcinomas
  • -Surgical cure is rare (the tumor has frequently already metastasized), but excision serves to
  • reduce the tumor mass and the degree of steroid hypersecretion
  • - Persisting nonsuppressible steroid secretion in the immediate postoperative period requires
  • treatment with Mitotane
  • Ectopic ACTH Syndrome
  • -Localizing and resecting ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors with node dissection as appropriate
  • is encouraged, whenever is possible. Bilateral adrenalectomy if the primary tumor is not
  • found (+ replacement therapy for life)
